observations.text: In Luke.11.9 zēteō is a direct imperative parallel to ask/knock, within its ordinary volitional-seeking sense; no divergence.
In Luke.11.24, zēteō (seeking) is role-T3, initiated by the unclean spirit and directed toward 'rest' as its sought object, in the waterless places it passes through.
In Luke.13.24 'many' (party) are the initiators of 'will seek' (zēteō) to enter the narrow door, directed toward the goal of entry itself; the operation fails because ability (ischyō) is lacking.
In Luke.13.24 'will seek to enter' matches the base gloss of striving/attempting -- straightforward volitional-effort sense with no special divergence.

In Luke.13.24 M23 (ischyō, 'able') co-occurs alongside M83 (zēteō, 'seek'). From M83's vantage, the seeking-to-enter precedes and is distinct from the capacity question raised by M23 -- many will seek entry but the text separates the act of seeking from the outcome of ability, so the two characteristics describe sequential but not overlapping aspects of the same event.

In John.1.38 M63 (hermēneuō, 'means/interpret') co-occurs with M83 (zēteō, 'seeking') but the two operate in separate clauses -- M83 governs Jesus' question to the followers, M63 explains the term 'Rabbi'; from M83's vantage the seeking-inquiry is unrelated to the interpretive gloss on the title.
In Luke.13.24 'will not be able' uses ischyō's standard modal-capacity sense ('to have power/be able'), matching the base gloss with no notable divergence.

Other M-code words present (M23 'bold') belong to a different cluster (boldness of Isaiah's speech) and are not directly related to the seeking-motif itself; the two operate on separate planes (Isaiah's boldness vs. the Gentiles' non-seeking).
No other M-code characteristic is present in John.5.18; the Jews' seeking-to-kill is the sole characteristic-bearing term in this verse within the cluster registry.
In John.5.18 the seeking-to-kill operation is initiated by 'the Jews' (party T11) and directed toward Jesus (party, implied by 'him'), driven by his Sabbath-breaking and equality-with-God claims.
In Matt.28.5 zēteō is used in its plain sense (the women's search for the crucified Jesus at the tomb); no divergence from base gloss.
In Mark.3.32 zēteō denotes the family's literal search for Jesus outside the crowd; plain sense, no divergence.

In Matt.28.5, M01 (fear, 'be not afraid') and M15 (knowledge, 'I know') co-occur with zēteō but are not directly tied to the seeking itself; the angel contrasts fear and knowledge against the women's search for Jesus, but zēteō's own role is simply to name what the women are doing, not to modify or be modified by the fear/knowledge terms.

In Mark.12.12, M01 (fear, 'feared the people') and M15 (perception, 'perceived') co-occur; the seeking-to-arrest is checked by fear of the crowd, but from zēteō's own vantage the seeking itself remains a distinct hostile-intent operation not merged with the fear/perception terms — it is thwarted by them rather than qualified by them.

In Luke.2.49, M15 (knowledge, 'did you not know') co-occurs with zēteō; Jesus's reply contrasts the parents' anxious seeking with a knowledge they lacked, implying the seeking arose from a gap in understanding rather than from malice — the seeking and knowledge terms are contrastively paired but not merged.
No other M-code characteristic co-occurs in Luke.13.7 alongside zēteō (fruit-seeking); the term stands as the verse's sole characteristic-bearing word.

In Luke.20.19, M01 (fear, 'feared the people') and M15 (perception, 'perceived') co-occur; as in Mark.12.12's parallel, the hostile seeking is restrained by the fear-term rather than combined with it — zēteō's own vantage is that the seeking-to-arrest remains the driving intent, checked externally by fear of the people.

In Matt.28.5, the operation-tagged word 'crucified' (role-T3) relates to the party Jesus (T7/T8) as the one who underwent it, initiated by unnamed crucifiers (implicit); this operation is distinct from but adjacent to the seeking-operation (zēteō) which the women (T2/T8 women) direct toward Jesus.

In Mark.3.32, the operation-tagged word 'sitting' (role-T3) is performed by the crowd around Jesus (party T2), while zēteō's own seeking-operation is initiated by the mother/brothers (party T8) directed toward Jesus (party T2) who is 'outside'.

In Acts 13:11 zeteo is used in its base literal sense — Paul, now blind, seeks people to lead him by the hand. This sits squarely within the ordinary physical 'look for/seek' gloss with no metaphorical or idiomatic shift.
In Matt.7.7, Matt.7.8, and Luke.11.10, no other M-code characteristic is tagged in the role list alongside G2212 -- it stands as the sole M-coded term in these verses.
Mark.14.55 'seeking testimony against Jesus' parallels Matt.26.59 within the base 'require/demand' sense, no additional divergence.
Luke.4.42: no other M-code characteristic co-occurs; the crowd's seeking of Jesus stands alone as the verse's characteristic content.

In John.6.24, M15 (saw, G1492H) co-occurs. Seeing (that Jesus was absent) is the triggering perception that produces the crowd's subsequent seeking; seeking here is the resultant action responding to a prior negative perception, not the same event as the perceiving.
In 1Cor 14:12 the seeking rendered 'strive' is done by the readers addressed and is aimed at excelling in building up the church.

Seeking/striving here is the drive that channels eagerness (M18, zeal for spiritual gifts, M47 Spirit) into concrete edification (building up, M52) of the church (M44); from seeking's vantage, it is the pivot converting inward zeal into outward communal benefit -- first relational pass for this verse.
Kinship stops strife or feeds it
How strife is kindled and quenched
Strife among believers is traced to an inner source
Anger in the lists
"How long?" Anger and compassion set against each other in a question.
Governed: slow, quick, ruled.
Another's anger turned or stirred; one word, two senses.
What ḥēmāh adds in the sayings: a person named by it.
The incensed are put to shame.
Strife: where it comes from, what holds it, what ends it.
Anger in the lists.
Where strife comes from.
The soul, the heart and the conscience turned toward the living God, or away.
Life loathed.
God called to awake when life is sought.

People select men for battle, leadership or a task, and the word marks fitness: "Moses chose able men out of all Israel and made them heads over the people" (Exo 18:25); "700 chosen men who were left-handed; every one could sling a stone at a hair and not miss" (Judg 20:16); "300,000 choice men, fit for war, able to handle spear and shield" (2Ch 25:5). The same word names the men "chosen from the assembly, well-known men" who rose up against Moses (Num 16:2).
eris, machē, Meribah: strife, fights, a place named for a quarrel (Gal 5:20; Jam 4:1; Exo 17:7; Psa 95:8). The quarrel stored in a place name, and read again as a hardened heart (S).
Form of anger, Strife and quarrel (27 / 25 hits and verses; faces 4Y, 4Z, 5W, 5X, 5Z; units 4, 5).
Form of anger, Governed in the sayings: slow, quick, turned, stirred (21 / 17 hits and verses; faces V, W, 2S; units 1, 2).
Form of anger, Put away and governed (the Greek lists and sayings) (19 / 13 hits and verses; faces 5L, 5M; units 5).

One root, different things: ʾaph: "pressing the nose produces blood, and pressing anger produces strife"; ḥēmāh: wrath, "the venom of asps", "the heat of wine"; ʿebrāh: wrath and "arrogant pride"; zāʿam: anger and "How can I denounce"; zāʿap̄: Uzziah's anger and "Why are your faces downcast today?"; ʿāšan: "Mount Sinai was wrapped in smoke" and "Why does your anger smoke"; kāʿas: provoking God and Hannah's "vexation"; thymos: God's "wrath" and Babylon's "passion"; paroxysmos: "a sharp disagreement" and "stir up one another to love".
God's anger leads to shame for those who burn against God and his people: "all who are incensed against you shall be put to shame and confounded".
A person's anger leads to strife: "A hot-tempered man stirs up strife"; "pressing anger produces strife"; "one given to anger causes much transgression".

Anger and Wickedness (M58); sin (M56): The cause named before the anger: "because of the evil of your deeds"; "Fret not yourself; it tends only to evil"; "one given to anger causes much transgression".
Anger and Shame (M07): "They shall be ashamed of their harvests because of the fierce anger"; the provocation is "to their own shame"; the incensed "put to shame"; Ezra "ashamed to ask the king".
Face W. Another's anger turned away or stirred: Hits / verses: 4 / 4; Who is angry, and at whom: the one who answers, gives or presses; Example verses: Pro 15:1; Pro 21:14; Pro 29:8; Pro 30:33.
The same word, two senses in one verse (new): "pressing the nose … pressing anger": Verses: Pro 30:33 (AG-52).
good sense → slow to anger (Pro 19:11); slow → quiets contention (15:18); quick → acts foolishly (14:17); given to anger → much transgression (29:22).
soft answer → wrath turned; harsh word → anger stirred (Pro 15:1); pressing anger → strife (Pro 30:33).

Face 2S. Wrath between people, in the sayings: Hits / verses: 10 / 10; Who, and at whom: the hot-tempered man, the man of wrath, the jealous husband, Esau; Example verses: Pro 15:1, 18; Pro 22:24; Pro 27:4; Pro 6:34; Gen 27:44.
hot-tempered → strife (Pro 15:18); man of wrath → strife (29:22); man of great wrath → penalty, deliver him → again (19:19); wrath → evil (Psa 37:8).

Face 3S. Enemies' anger, as the one attacked bears it: Hits / verses: 4 / 4; Who, and at whom: enemies, Rezin and Syria, "all who are incensed"; Example verses: Psa 124:3; Isa 7:4; Isa 41:11; Isa 45:24.
foes → eye wastes away (Psa 6:7); toil → vexation → heart does not rest at night (Ecc 2:22–23).

Face 4Y. Strife and quarrel between people: Hits / verses: 8 / 8; Who, and at whom: the one who sows discord, the quarrelsome man, the meddler, a backbiting tongue; Abram and Lot; Example verses: Gen 13:8; Pro 6:14; Pro 18:19; Pro 26:21.

perverted heart → sowing discord (Pro 6:14); quarrelsome man → kindling strife (26:21); no whisperer → quarreling ceases (26:20); tarry over wine → strife, wounds (23:29–30); backbiting tongue → angry looks (25:23); no strife, for we are kinsmen → choose the land (Gen 13:8–9).
16 verses hold two or three of the Greek anger words (for example Eph 4:31 and Col 3:8, orgē with thymos; Gal 5:20, three words); no verse of the unit holds a Hebrew word from units 1 to 4.
Face 5L. Anger in the lists of what is put away: Hits / verses: 11 / 6; Who, and at whom: people; no object named; Example verses: Gal 5:20; Eph 4:31; Col 3:8; 2Cor 12:20; Rom 1:29; Rom 13:13.

Face 5W. Strife among believers, and its source: Hits / verses: 12 / 10; Who, and at whom: believers, the conceited, those who cause divisions; at one another; Example verses: Jam 4:1; 1Cor 1:11; 1Cor 3:3; 1Ti 6:4–5; Tit 3:9; 2Ti 2:23; Gal 5:26; Phili 1:15; Rom 16:17.

passions at war within → quarrels and fights (Jam 4:1); covet, cannot obtain → fight and quarrel (4:2); jealousy and strife → of the flesh (1Cor 3:3); conceit, craving → quarrels about words → envy, dissension, slander (1Ti 6:4); controversies → breed quarrels (2Ti 2:23).

In the vice lists with thumos (2Cor 12:20; Gal 5:20; Eph 4:31; Col 3:8) the inner place is given by the list's frame, not by a seat: in Gal 5:19 anger is among "the works of the flesh", with 5:17 (flesh against Spirit) nearby; in Col 3:8 it is put away along with speech "from your mouth"; flesh and mouth take the seat's place.

The strife words are mostly in vice lists and church-order texts, where the inner place is given by the frame: 1Cor 3:3, "you are still of the flesh"; 1Ti 6:4-5, "puffed up with conceit ... depraved in mind" (nous is excluded from M47 by ruling 4, so these do not count as seated); Gal 5:26 ("provoking one another, envying one another") sits between 5:24-25 (flesh crucified, walk by the Spirit) and 6:1.
Gen 13:8: "Let there be no strife between you and me ... for we are kinsmen": strife refused on the ground of kinship.

"Slow to anger" (Pro 14:29; 15:18; 16:32; 19:11) is literally "long of nostrils", the same idiom as God's self-description in Exo 34:6 (Num 14:18; Neh 9:17; Psa 86:15; 103:8; 145:8; Jon 4:2; Nah 1:3): a human virtue and a divine attribute share one body idiom.

Pro 20:2, "The terror of a king is like the growling of a lion; whoever provokes him to anger forfeits his life", sets the fear of a ruler beside the anger of the ruler and says what provoking him costs; the verse after says what to do instead, "It is an honor for a man to keep aloof from strife, but every fool will be quarreling" (20:3), and the verse before names wine as "a brawler" (20:1).

Ecc 1:16–17 "I said in my heart … I applied my heart to know". Genuine. The bearer's own (E v2 §1.3; B v3 §1.2, §1.11; C v3 §10). New here is only the link: the heart that seeks knowledge comes before the vexation that knowledge brings.
Psa 7:5 "let the enemy pursue my soul". Genuine / life.
Scarcity: "the land could not support both of them" (Gen 13:6), and "strife between the herdsmen" (13:7).

What it does: Abram refuses it: "Let there be no strife between you and me … for we are kinsmen" (Gen 13:8); God forbids it: "Do not harass Moab … because I have given Ar to the people of Lot" (Deu 2:9). Likewise Ammon, "the sons of Lot" (Deu 2:19); The men of Judah and Israel fight over the king with kinship as the weapon: "Because the king is our close relative. Why then are you angry over this matter?" (2Sa 19:42).

Where it comes from: Scarcity: "the land could not support both of them" (Gen 13:6), and "strife between the herdsmen" (13:7); Rival claims on a person: "Why have our brothers the men of Judah stolen you away?" (2Sa 19:41).

Part 2 verses: what they add. Three new strands: (a) The eye wasting, as in Job 17:7; "My eye wastes away because of grief; it grows weak because of all my foes" (Psa 6:7), after "every night I flood my bed with tears" (6:6); "My eye is wasted from grief; my soul and my body also. For my life is spent with sorrow" (Psa 31:9–10); The eye is where ka'as shows in the body, in all three texts (Job 17:7; Psa 6:7; 31:9); What turns Psa 6 round is being heard: "the Lord has heard the sound of my weeping. The Lord has heard my plea" (6:8–9). In Psa 10:14, "you do see, for you note mischief and vexation, that you may take it into your hands; to you the helpless commits himself". The vexation is seen by God, and the helpless hands it over; (b) Provocation from those closest; "A foolish son is a grief to his father and bitterness to her who bore him" (Pro 17:25); The reverse direction: "Fathers, do not provoke your children to anger" (Eph 6:4), and "do not provoke your children, lest they become discouraged" (Col 3:21); Vexation passes both ways between parent and child. Col 3:21 names its outcome as losing heart. Hannah's rival (1Sa 1:6) was a co-wife. These are the family members; (c) Qoheleth's vexation: the vexation of the thinker and the worker; Knowing brings it: "in much wisdom is much vexation, and he who increases knowledge increases sorrow" (Ecc 1:18). This comes after "I applied my heart to know wisdom … this also is but a striving after wind" (1:17); Work brings it, and it keeps the heart awake: "his work is a vexation. Even in the night his heart does not rest" (2:23); "all his days he eats in darkness in much vexation and sickness and anger" (5:17); Its answer is enjoyment received as God's gift: "There is nothing better … than that he should eat and drink and find enjoyment in his toil. This also, I saw, is from the hand of God" (2:24), and "this is the gift of God" (5:19); It is to be removed: "Remove vexation from your heart, and put away pain from your body" (11:10), after "Rejoice, O young man … let your heart cheer you" (11:9); It is sometimes better than laughter: "Sorrow [ka'as] is better than laughter, for by sadness of face the heart is made glad" (7:3). The one place where ka'as is valued. The face is sad and the heart made good. Face and heart go in opposite directions.

Where it comes from. Every verse, or the one next to it, names a source, and the sources are inner: Passions at war within: "What causes quarrels and what causes fights among you? Is it not this, that your passions are at war within you? You desire and do not have, so you murder. You covet and cannot obtain, so you fight and quarrel" (Jam 4:1–2). The outer fight is the inner war carried outward; The flesh: "for you are still of the flesh. For while there is jealousy and strife among you, are you not of the flesh and behaving only in a human way?" (1Cor 3:3), after "I could not address you as spiritual people, but as people of the flesh" (3:1); Conceit: "Let us not become conceited, provoking one another, envying one another" (Gal 5:26). "He is puffed up with conceit and understands nothing. He has an unhealthy craving for controversy" (1Ti 6:4); Appetite: the dividers "do not serve our Lord Christ, but their own appetites [belly]" (Rom 16:18); Envy and selfish ambition behind a good act: "Some indeed preach Christ from envy and rivalry, but others from good will … The former proclaim Christ out of selfish ambition, not sincerely but thinking to afflict me" (Phili 1:15–17). The same outward act, preaching, has opposite inner sources; A depraved mind: "constant friction among people who are depraved in mind and deprived of the truth, imagining that godliness is a means of gain" (1Ti 6:5); Controversies themselves: "foolish, ignorant controversies … breed quarrels" (2Ti 2:23); "avoid foolish controversies, genealogies, dissensions, and quarrels about the law" (Tit 3:9).

How it co-exists: With envy, often (5 of the 11 verses). Envy is paired with strife in Gal 5:26; Phili 1:15; 1Ti 6:4; 1Cor 3:3 ("jealousy"); in Jam 4:2 it is "covet"; With its named opposites: "that there be no divisions among you, but that you be united in the same mind and the same judgment" (1Cor 1:10); "godliness with contentment is great gain" (1Ti 6:6); "the Lord's servant must not be quarrelsome but kind to everyone … correcting his opponents with gentleness" (2Ti 2:24–25); "keep in step with the Spirit" (Gal 5:25).

What it does, in the sayings' own images: Fuel: "As charcoal to hot embers and wood to fire, so is a quarrelsome man for kindling strife" (26:21), and the verse before: "For lack of wood the fire goes out, and where there is no whisperer, quarreling ceases" (26:20); Pressure: "pressing milk produces curds, pressing the nose produces blood, and pressing anger produces strife" (30:33). The "nose" is aph itself: squeeze the anger-nose and blood comes; Weather: "The north wind brings forth rain, and a backbiting tongue, angry looks" (25:23); Danger to the meddler: "Whoever meddles in a quarrel not his own is like one who takes a passing dog by the ears" (26:17).

Where it comes from: The angry person: "A hot-tempered man stirs up strife" (15:18); "A man of wrath stirs up strife, and one given to anger causes much transgression" (29:22); The evil heart: "with perverted heart devises evil, continually sowing discord" (6:14); The tongue: a backbiting tongue (25:23), and the whisperer (26:20, 22); Wine: "Who has strife? Who has complaining? … Those who tarry long over wine" (23:29–30).

What it does. It stands among its companions: "envy, murder, strife, deceit" (Rom 1:29); "quarreling and jealousy" (Rom 13:13); "quarreling, jealousy, anger, hostility, slander, gossip, conceit, and disorder" (2Cor 12:20); "enmity, strife, jealousy, fits of anger, rivalries, dissensions, divisions, envy" (Gal 5:20–21); "bitterness and wrath and anger and clamor and slander … malice" (Eph 4:31); "anger, wrath, malice, slander, and obscene talk from your mouth" (Col 3:8).

What it leads to. Deliverance, looked back on or asked for: "If it had not been the Lord who was on our side" (Psa 124:1–2); "you stretch out your hand against the wrath of my enemies, and your right hand delivers me" (138:7); "all who are incensed against you shall be put to shame" (Isa 41:11), after "fear not, for I am with you" (41:10); "God, who comforts the downcast, comforted us by the coming of Titus" (2Cor 7:6).

Seat: In the verse: 2Cor 7:5 "bodies" (sarx, flesh). The bearer's own, bodily: "no rest". Not in any batch: new. The inner state is carried by "fear within", not by the seat word; Outside the verse:; Psa 55:4 "My heart is in anguish within me". Genuine. The attacked one's own; Psa 58:2 and 140:2 "hearts … heart". Genuine. The enemy's own, where the wrong is devised; Psa 7:5 "let the enemy pursue my soul". Genuine / life; 2Cor 7:3 "you are in our hearts". Genuine. The bearer's own, holding others. Not in any batch; So the seat appears on both sides: the enemy's heart that devises, and the attacked one's heart that is in anguish.

VX §8 (Psa 10:14; 31:9; Ecc 1:18; 2:23; 7:3; 11:10; Col 3:21; Eph 6:4): Context seats: sense · batch · use: Psa 10:13 "say in his heart": offender's · C v3 §9.4 · used. Psa 31:7 "distress of my soul": bearer's own · E v2 §10.1 · used. Ecc 1:16–17 heart · E v2 §1.3, B v3 §1.2 · used. Ecc 2:22 heart · new · used. Ecc 2:24 "find" [make his soul see good] · new · used (enjoyment as answer). Ecc 5:16 "wind" · spurious. Ecc 7:2, 7:4 heart · A v3 §3.3 · used. Ecc 11:9 heart · F v4 §7, H v1 §4.1 · used. Eph 6:5–6, Col 3:22–23 "heart … heartily" (bondservants) · E v2 §6, H v1 §3.1 · not used (next household rule).

EA §28: Context seats: sense · batch · use: Psa 7:5 soul · F v4 §8.4 et al. · used. Psa 55:4 heart · A v3 §1, G v3 §16.3 · used. Psa 58:2; 140:2 hearts · F v4 §12.2 et al. · used. Psa 124:4–5 "us" · spurious (pilot §0). 2Cor 7:3 "in our hearts" · new · used.

What it does: Why? "O God, why do you cast us off forever? Why does your anger smoke against the sheep of your pasture?" (Psa 74:1); How long? "How long, O Lord? Will you be angry forever?" (79:5); "how long will you be angry with your people's prayers?" (80:4); "How long, O Lord? Will you hide yourself forever? How long will your wrath burn like fire?" (89:46); Restore. "you have been angry; oh, restore us" (60:1); "Restore us again, O God of our salvation, and put away your indignation toward us!" (85:4).
(v3) 1Th 2:16 (RB): Context seat: 1Th 2:17 "in person not in heart"; Whose · check: Paul's · genuine; Already read in: C v3 §1.3, §4; §: §9.

zîd and zādôn name a pride that acts where it was not sent: Speaking what God did not say. "the prophet who presumes to speak a word in my name that I have not commanded him" (Deu 18:20). Such a word fails, and "You need not be afraid of him" (18:22). Presumption here borrows God's name for its own word; Going up when told not to. "Do not go up ... So I spoke to you, and you would not listen; but you rebelled against the command of the Lord and presumptuously went up" (Deu 1:42–43). It came straight after "We have sinned ... We ourselves will go up" (1:41). After the defeat, "you returned and wept before the Lord" (1:45). I read: presumption can wear the clothes of repentance. It goes up when the moment to go up has passed; Not obeying; Not obeying the priest or judge (Deu 17:12). The rest "shall hear and fear and not act presumptuously again" (17:13); "they ... acted presumptuously and stiffened their neck and did not obey your commandments. They ... were not mindful of the wonders that you performed" (Neh 9:16–17); "you warned them in order to turn them back ... Yet they acted presumptuously" (9:29); Joined to these are a stiff neck, a stubborn shoulder, and forgetting the wonders. Each time God's mercy answers: "But you are a God ready to forgive" (9:17); Kept from it. "Keep back your servant also from presumptuous sins; let them not have dominion over me!" (Psa 19:13). It follows "Who can discern his errors?" (19:12). Presumption is asked to be kept from, as something that would rule; Not hearing; "Hear and give ear; be not proud, for the Lord has spoken" (Jer 13:15); "By insolence comes nothing but strife, but with those who take advice is wisdom" (Pro 13:10); "When pride comes, then comes disgrace, but with the humble is wisdom" (Pro 11:2, carried); The opposite named for pride is hearing, taking advice, humility; The fool. "a fool is reckless and careless", against the wise who "is cautious and turns away from evil" (Pro 14:16); Scoffing. "'Scoffer' is the name of the arrogant, haughty man who acts with arrogant pride" (Pro 21:24); Intent. "if a man willfully attacks another to kill him by cunning" (Exo 21:14). It is set against the one who "did not lie in wait for him" (21:13). Here the word names intent carried out against another; Pride named wrongly; Eliab, angry: "I know your presumption and the evil of your heart". David answers: "What have I done now? Was it not but a word?" (1Sa 17:28–29); The passage shows David asking about the one who defies "the armies of the living God" (17:26); I read: the charge of presumption here comes from an older brother's anger. The verses do not show it to be true.
"A greedy man stirs up strife, but the one who trusts in the Lord will be enriched" (Pro 28:25). The word's gloss is "broad: arrogant"; ESV has "greedy". It bears on M18.

Proverbs paints the scoffer by what he will not receive: Rebuke; "A wise son hears his father's instruction, but a scoffer does not listen to rebuke" (Pro 13:1); "A scoffer does not like to be reproved; he will not go to the wise" (15:12). The verse before is "Sheol and Abaddon lie open before the Lord; how much more the hearts of the children of man!" (15:11); Hatred of correction. "Whoever corrects a scoffer gets himself abuse ... Do not reprove a scoffer, or he will hate you; reprove a wise man, and he will love you" (Pro 9:7–8). The same rebuke brings out hate in one and love in the other; Wisdom in vain. "A scoffer seeks wisdom in vain, but knowledge is easy for a man of understanding" (Pro 14:6). He seeks, and does not find; Learning by his fall; "Strike a scoffer, and the simple will learn prudence" (19:25); "When a scoffer is punished, the simple becomes wise" (21:11); The scoffer is not the one who learns. Others learn from what happens to him; Strife. "Drive out a scoffer, and strife will go out, and quarreling and abuse will cease" (Pro 22:10). "the scoffer is an abomination to mankind" (24:9); Justice and the guilt offering; "A worthless witness mocks at justice" (19:28). "Condemnation is ready for scoffers" (19:29); "Fools mock at the guilt offering, but the upright enjoy acceptance" (14:9). They mock the very means of putting guilt right; Delight, and the offer. "How long will scoffers delight in their scoffing ... If you turn at my reproof, behold, I will pour out my spirit to you" (Pro 1:22–23). Scoffing is a delight held on to, and the offer still stands to the one who turns; Alone. "If you are wise, you are wise for yourself; if you scoff, you alone will bear it" (Pro 9:12); The seat. "Blessed is the man who ... nor sits in the seat of scoffers; but his delight is in the law of the Lord" (Psa 1:1–2). The scoffer's seat is set against delight in the law; The warning; "do not scoff, lest your bonds be made strong", then "Give ear, and hear my voice" (Isa 28:22–23). The Hebrew strife nouns (H4066, H4079, H4090, H4683, H4695) are genuine domestic and social discord, the family's only real match to the cluster's apparent theme, overwhelmingly Proverbs material: hot temper, wrath and greed are strife's stated causes (Prov 15:18, 29:22, 28:25).

Who rouses, and whom. God rouses himself (Zec 2:13). People call on God to rouse himself (Psa 44:23). God rouses a human spirit (Ezr 1:1). God rouses people against people (2Ch 21:16; Eze 23:22). A person rouses himself, or does not (Isa 64:7). Hatred rouses strife (Pro 10:12). An angel rouses a prophet from sleep (Zec 4:1). Love is not to be roused before its time (Song 2:7).

Toward what. The same verb rouses toward building (Ezr 1:5; Hag 1:14), toward destruction (Jer 51:1, 11), toward praise (Psa 57:8; Judg 5:12), toward hearing (Isa 50:4), and toward strife (Pro 10:12).

What thoughts are: Design: forming something that does not yet exist. H2803G (19 rows) describes craftsmanship: cherubim "skillfully worked" (Exod 26:1, 31) and "skilled design" (Exod 39:3). The faculty itself is neutral. *Maḥăšāvāh* covers both artistry and plots, and *mᵊzimmāh* covers both "discretion" (Prov 2:11) and "evil devices" (Prov 12:2). What makes a thought good or evil is what it is designed toward.; Reckoning: giving something its value or category. H2803H/J (60 rows): Human misreckoning: Eli "took her to be a drunken woman" (1 Sam 1:13), "we esteemed him stricken" and "we esteemed him not" (Isa 53:3–4), Judah "thought she was a prostitute" (Gen 38:15).; God's reckoning: "he counted it to him as righteousness" (Gen 15:6), "the Lord counts no iniquity" (Ps 32:2), and the nations "accounted as the dust on the scales" (Isa 40:15, 17).; To think is to judge the worth of something, and people can judge wrongly.; Inner speech.; "all his thoughts are, 'There is no God'" (Ps 10:4). The thought is quoted as a sentence.; Hannah "was speaking in her heart; only her lips moved" (1 Sam 1:13).; *Dialogismos* covers both inner reasoning and outward "argument", "quarreling" and "disputing".; "conflicting thoughts accuse or even excuse" (Rom 2:15).; Something that affects the body and emotions.; "his thoughts alarmed him; his limbs gave way, and his knees knocked together" (Dan 5:6; also 4:19; 5:10; 7:28).; "the cares of my heart" (Ps 94:19), and "haste within me" (Job 20:2).; A divided mind stalls a person: "limping between two different opinions" (1 Kgs 18:21, H5587A).; Creaturely and passing.; "but a breath" (Ps 94:11).; "When his breath departs … on that very day his plans perish" (Ps 146:4).; "futile" (1 Cor 3:20; Rom 1:21).; "striving of heart … striving after wind" (Eccl 2:22; 4:16).
Quietness is itself the settled inner rest and trust: the result of righteousness, the ground of strength, and better than toil and striving.
Called here only names, designates or labels a person, place or thing (to be called such a name, to call it so); no inner-being operation is voiced by it.
Anger is here the anger, wrath, rage or fury of a person or people: a state of the heart aroused against another, a thing or God, named by the word itself.

Angry is here the anger, wrath or fury of God against persons or nations (kindled, poured out, turned away, executed, provoked); it is God's own act upon them, and bears on their inner response, which other words of the verse name, if at all.
Madness is here madness or derangement of the mind or heart: a state of the inner being, set against wisdom or sanity, or a craze such as a passion for idols.
Wrath is here the anger, wrath, rage or fury of a person or people: a state of the heart aroused against another, a thing or God, named by the word itself.

Holiness is here the godliness, devoutness, reverence or uprightness of a person as a state of the heart toward God or toward what is right (a devout man who feared God, godliness trained and pursued, uprightness of heart, reverence and awe).

Wicked is here the godly, the righteous, the upright, the wicked or the ungodly as a class of persons toward whom an act is directed or whom an event befalls (the Lord keeps the godly, do not envy the wicked, Christ died for the ungodly); the act is named by another word of the verse.

Choose is here a person's own act of choosing or deciding: a purposeful act of the will that picks one thing, way, person or course over another (choose life, choose whom you will serve, decided in his heart, Mary has chosen the good portion).
Arise here is bodily rising, going or acting, or something coming into being, or God arising; no human inner-being operation is qualified.
Complaining names the inner operation of voicing grievance, set among woe, sorrow and strife.
Shelter here is a hiding place, a refuge from storm or enemy, God as shelter, or a roof; no human inner-being operation is named or qualified.
Trample here is trampling on the poor, beasts or a city with feet or hoofs, or being trampled by enemies; an outward act, no inner-being operation is named or qualified.

'seek' is here a desire or purpose of the will directed to an object (glory, wisdom, peace, a sign, rest, favour, one's own good, or a turning to other gods), good or ill; the direction of the will is what 'seek' names.
In Ecc 2:11 'considered' is the Preacher turning to look over all his hands had done and the toil spent: a survey of his works that ends in the verdict that all was vanity.

Considering a matter: turning attention and thought to it, looking it over, setting the heart on it. The Lord asks Satan whether he has fixed on Job, the observer sets his heart on the field and takes instruction, the Preacher looks over all his works, the generation gives no thought to the servant's being cut off, the sinner sees his transgressions and turns, the seer contemplates the horns, Joseph turns over what he resolved, and Abraham fixes his attention on his own body without his faith weakening. In each the consideration is an act of the mind taking in a matter, usually before a turn or a conclusion. Verses: Job 1:8, Job 2:3, Pro 24:32, Ecc 2:11, Isa 53:8, Eze 18:28, Dan 7:8, Mat 1:20, Rom 4:19.

The codes of considering are verbs of setting, turning and looking: H7760K and H7896K (to put, set; set mind to), H6437G (to turn), H7200H (to see, consider), H7878 (to muse), H7920 (to consider, contemplate), G2657 (to pay attention, contemplate, with intense attention) and G1760 (to reflect on). With them H3820A (heart) is the seat set on the matter, as in Job 1:8 and Pro 24:32. The lexicon bears out attention set on a matter and taken in. H0595 (I), H1934 (to be) and G3756 (not) are small words in the units of Pro 24:32, Dan 7:8 and Rom 4:19.

The surface considered carries many codes in two uses. Of attention set on a matter: H7760K with H3820A in Job 1:8 and Job 2:3 (set the heart), H7896K in Pro 24:32, H6437G in Ecc 2:11, H7878 in Isa 53:8, H7200H in Eze 18:28, H7920 in Dan 7:8, G1760 in Mat 1:20, G2657 in Rom 4:19. Of counting as something: H2803H in 1Ki 10:21, 2Ch 9:20 and Neh 13:13, H2803J in Pro 17:28, G1380 in Mar 10:42, G2233 in Heb 11:11 and Heb 11:26, G3049 in Heb 11:19. H0595, H1934 and G3756 are small words in the units.
In Ecc 2:11 gained (H3504) stands thirteen words after considered, at the end of what the considering found: nothing to be gained under the sun.
In Ecc 2:11 toil (H5999) stands four words after considered as what is considered: the toil the Preacher spent.

In 1Sa 1:16 Hannah asks Eli not to regard her as a worthless woman, and in 1Sa 25:25 Abigail asks David not to regard Nabal: regarding is counting a person as worthless. In Job 37:24 God does not regard the wise in their own conceit: conceit is what he withholds regard from. In Ecc 2:11 the Preacher considered all his toil, and it was vanity.
In Ecc 2:11 the Preacher considered all his work and toil and found it vanity and a striving after wind: the considering is a review of his toil that reaches its verdict.

In Pro 24:32, Ecc 2:11, Eze 18:28, Dan 7:8, Rom 4:19 and Mat 1:20 considering is attention set on a matter and taken in: the field looked over, the toil surveyed, the transgressions seen, the horns watched, the body faced, the things Joseph turned over. The person does it, and it comes before a turn, a verdict or a word from God.
In Ecc 2:11 the considering of all the work and toil ends in a verdict: all was vanity and nothing was gained.

Attending: turning the mind to a matter and dwelling on it. The operation is the same in every element: a person sets the mind on a matter and stays with it (meditate, ponder, consider, give thought, think on). It runs through four subgroups. What differs is the object (God's law and works, one's ways, a field, the toil of a life, the word), the mode (done, resolved, commanded, denied, lacking) and where it leads; those differences are kept as relating findings R1 and R4, not as separate behaviours.
